justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish near-term bias anchored around the S&P 500's recent trading levels. At the one-day horizon, I placed the estimate near 490.5, assuming mean-reversion tendencies and the absence of major overnight catalysts would keep price action contained close to the prior close. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 492, reflecting a mild upward drift assumption consistent with the long-run equity risk premium and the absence of clear near-term macro headwinds. At the one-month horizon, I moved to 496, incorporating a slightly larger drift component while acknowledging that a full month gives more time for fundamental developments to materialize. In all three cases, the estimates are fairly close together because we are already in a relatively range-bound environment and I did not have strong directional conviction.

The confidence interval widths grow predictably with the forecast horizon, reflecting the square-root-of-time scaling typical in financial volatility modeling. At one day, realized volatility in the S&P 500 tends to run around 1–1.5% on an average session, which justifies the tight 481–500 band. By one week, multiple daily moves compound, widening the range to roughly 474–510. By one month, I allowed for considerably more dispersion, reflecting that macro surprises, earnings, and Federal Reserve communications can accumulate and shift sentiment meaningfully. Implied volatility levels from options markets were a key input here, as they encode market participants' collective uncertainty about near-term outcomes.

There are meaningful tail risks that could push outcomes well outside my stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in U.S. labor markets, a credit event in commercial real estate or regional banking, or an escalation in geopolitical conflicts could trigger a risk-off move of 5–10% or more, breaking below the lower bound easily. On the upside, a dovish pivot surprise from the Federal Reserve, a stronger-than-expected earnings season, or a de-escalation of trade tensions could push equities meaningfully above 533 within the month. Liquidity conditions and positioning also matter — if markets are crowded in one direction, the unwind can be faster and larger than volatility models suggest.

Finally, I want to be transparent that these forecasts carry substantial model uncertainty. Equity markets in the short run are close to unpredictable, and point estimates at a one-day or one-week horizon are only marginally more informative than the current price itself.
